As a first step the child should take the parent aside and point out the economic facts of life, so that bills of this nature would not be brought before Parliament. The Commission should point out to the government the need for keeping its taxes, tax increases and spending growth to a minimum for the next two years, or at least until inflation is under control. In the public sector one of the problems faced by the Commission is that the people with whom it discusses inflation are not threatened directly by tough federal, fiscal or monetary policies. In fact, the government has what I would call a cream-puff policy toward inflation.
The government's present taxation policies cause the burden of unemployment to fall mainly on the low-income group. They are the ones who today are being asked to carry the heaviest load. Executives, civil servants, doctors, lawyers, and even labour leaders are in a strong position to keep their incomes ahead of inflation. None of the people in these classes is likely to be thrown out of work by what economists predict will be a more severe recession in 1970 than that which we are facing in 1969.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The Prices and Incomes Commission is therefore arguing its case for urgency that inflation be cured to a group that is still unconvinced that the problems of inflation and the consequences of announced government restraint are vital and urgent. One of the things we do not need is another study of inflation in order to advise the government how it can avoid another wage-price spiral in our economy. Surely the facts behind mounting inflation are now well known to the government and its supporters. What is now called for by the majority of Canadians is leadership and action and an indication of real economies in government operations. Anyone can increase taxes, and that is what the bill before us proposes to do. That is what it is, Mr. Speaker-an increase in taxes.
Hear, hear.

The Canadian people expected this load to be taken off their backs. They were foolish enough to believe the then minister of finance when he stated this surtax

December 11, 1969
Income Tax Act
would apply only for the years 1969 and 1970. I say, Mr. Speaker, they are an increase in taxes.
When speaking on this matter on March 7, 1968, the then minister of finance, Mr. Sharp, said: ".. .the measures proposed in this resolution are intended to produce $390 million in budgetary revenues in the 1968-69 fiscal year." Yet today when this measure was introduced to the House by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), he almost implied that we should pass it quickly-let's get this over in a hurry; it is only a small matter! From the wording of the bill one might suppose it is quite innocuous, that it does not have any great effect on Canada, but we cannot ignore any measure which proposes to take $390 million out of the Canadian economy and divert it to the government sector. The application of these taxes to the over-all development of Canada demonstrates, in the final analysis, the administrative ability of a government. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the extension of these surtaxes for another year is a frank admission that this government is giving weak and ineffective leadership in its efforts to curb inflation.
Hear, hear.

We can only hope that the men who occupy the treasury benches will read the Financial Post and the Financial Times and learn what is going on in Canada. We have regional desks and I do not know what they are doing, but obviously there is a great space between the grass and the brass because they are not aware of what is happening in this country. We hope they will have such a realization very shortly and will bring in policies that will not create stagnation in our economy but will instead bring over-all growth and development to Canada. It is time this government showed its concern for stability in our economy; it is time this government showed some concern for increasing employment, not unemployment, in our labour force. By that I do not mean, Mr. Speaker, advertisements of the type I saw in the press this week extolling the benefits of being unemployed. That is not the kind of advertisement that built this country, and it is not what we want to see in our press, publicizing the inability of this government and its desire to bring in policies to keep people out of work, emphasizing the benefits of the dole.
Shame!

Only when we bring back stability and growth to this economy, only when these prime objectives are achieved, can the government hope to attain some of its socialistic dreams. This will not be achieved, Mr. Speaker, by saying one thing and doing another, which was done by a former minister of finance, as reported in Hansard. It will not be achieved by making false promises to the people of Canada in an effort to buy time to use as a cover-up for inaction regarding the basic problems facing Canadians.
Inflation is the major problem today. The stability of our economy and the reduction of regional disparities should be the government's major goal. The puck is on the government side, and rather than watch some fancy stickhandling over there by individual players, let us see a team effort to solve our problems. Team effort, Mr. Speaker, is in the final analysis the only effort with any chance of success. For these reasons I am happy to second the motion moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).

Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I will infringe for only a second the rules of the house, because of the outright provocation directed to me by the opposition by referring to Three Rivers.
This is not a matter of narrow-mindedness nor of out and out nationalism; it is that there is no such city as Three Rivers. In fact, we still have the English version of the incorporation act of the city of Trois-Rivieres, where it is actually called Trois-Rivieres.
By the way, I urge all members from other provinces to name cities having incorporation acts written in both languages, dating back to more than a hundred years, as in the case of Trois-Rivieres.
For instance, there is in Manitoba a city called Souris and nobody ever thought of translating that into Mouse. The Speaker's name is Lamoureux, yet I never call him Lover.
I have a few words to add concerning Bill C-139, for it would be unthinkable to leave Hansard readers under the impression that the wave of curses that has just unfurled on the party in power is justified. There are, after all, obvious principles, even for the opposition members, but they are not in a position to say so, because it would not be cricket.
December 11, 1969

Everybody understands that it is not pleasant to maintain a tax, no more than to pay it. Everybody understands that it is not pleasant for anyone to undergo a painful operation or to deprive oneself of things one is most anxious to have, because one cannot afford them. But that is a part of the sacrifices people and individuals must bear to avoid a greater evil.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
What does history teach us? A while ago, an hon. member quoted the memorable remark of the then minister of finance: "This 3 per cent surtax will apply only for the taxation years 1968 and 1969". Of course, he was speaking in good faith, according to information provided him by experts.
For instance, no opposition member can forecast next year's weather on this same date. One cannot guarantee what the economic climate will be in Canada or elsewhere a year from now, taking into account the crisis we are going through presently. Hon. members of the opposition know that Canada is now experiencing the same difficulties as almost all the industrialized countries of the West.
We have only to remember what happened in England and in France, and the situation there was infinitely more serious than it is in Canada. It even led to the overthrow of a giant in France. We can also see today what is happening in Italy. I will not speak of less fortunate countries which have been facing economic hardships for centuries.
It is an international phenomenon, but fortunately the government has taken up the challenge and prevented greater harm. It has even been able to find solutions.
I remember the vote we took in early March of 1968. I was sitting at the other end of the House. I was sitting as an independent for personal reasons which the electors of my constituency understood. However, they warned me: we do not elect you as an independent to systematically fight the government. We elect you to support the government when it is right and to make representations to it when it is wrong. When the vote was taken on the 3 per cent tax increase I had decided to vote against it. I had even advised my fellow-citizens that I would vote against it.
But a few days before the vote was taken, an international crisis arose on which my hon. friends are aware. I am not as learned as the universal experts we have heard tonight, and
Income Tax Act
I am not a quack that tries to impose panaceas. When I do not have sufficient knowledge about a subject, I consult the experts. Well then, I consulted some Canadian and American financiers who told me: "We are going through a crisis so severe that if the government does not take strong measures, the Canadian and the American dollar might be devalued."
That is when we proceeded with a major operation. Therefore, I explained to my fellow-citizens why I had changed my mind. Anyhow, only imbeciles do not change their minds.
Why did I change my mind then? Because it was in the best interest of the Canadian nation. I take this opportunity to pay a tribute to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield); indeed, one day, he could have defeated the government. He had only to say so and the Liberal government would have been defeated. But he refused, in spite of the advice of some members of his party, to contribute to the defeat of the government, because he remembered that Lincoln had said: It is not best to swap horses while crossing the river. One does not rock the boat in the midst of a storm.
When the well-being of a nation is concerned, all political considerations should be put aside to support the government which is in fact that of our country. That is what the Leader of the Opposition did last year, disregarding the advice of some of his own members, and I have admired him a little more on that account.
As for myself, I have supported the governmental policy, because it has stood the test of time. To prove my point, I shall not bring forward my own testimony, but rather quote from a summary of the Sixth Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada, "Perspective 1975", published in September 1969. I admit that the austerity policy of the government has been painful. It required some sacrifices, but the Canadian people understood. My electors understood so well that after giving me a majority of 2000 votes in 1965, they gave me one of about 7000 in the 1968 election.
On page 27 of this summary, we can read the following:
Up to the mid-1970's, Canada's rate of growth should keep going up sharply and even exceed in that respect the performance of most Industrialized nations.

December 11, 1969
Income Tax Act
And 1 do emphasize these words:
-exceed ... the performance of most industrialized nations. Under such conditions, the welfare of the Canadian people will be greatly increased.
In the Review of the Economic Council of Canada, the authors do not deal in partisan politics but rather analyze carefully the situation prevailing in September 1969, as a result of the measures taken in the string of 1968.
A little further on, we can read on page 29 of the report, and I quote:
The success of the proposed measures, especially in the case of monetary policy, will depend upon the implementation of comparable measures in the United States.
I should now like to remind opposition members that it took over a year and a half to agree to that surtax, then a 10 per cent increase was imposed and it is that supplement we are still discussing now. In fact, it was the opinion of most of American economists then that the United States had missed the boat because they had passed this measure at least a year too late.
The quotation goes on:
It seems that, while moving away from the previous policy which was mainly geared to the short term cyclical fluctuations, this country is heading more and more towards longer term programs similar to those which we have been advocating for Canada.
This being so, our country will be prompted and encouraged to adopt similar measures.
And a little further, Mr. Speaker, we can read the following, and I quote:
For the fifth consecutive year, the public accounts established on the basis of the national accounts and including all sectors of government (including the revenue derived from the pension plans), show a surplus in 1968. We must note that for that year, this surplus was achieved at a time when the economy was slowing down a little while the unemployment rate was getting near 5 per cent. Had there been full employment, this surplus would have been sensibly more important. From 1969 on, austerity measures far more severe than in the United States were introduced in the budgetary policy, as shown by our analysis of the national accounts. It will be necessary to watch closely the opportunity of maintaining those restraints applied by the Canadian government at all levels.
Indeed, the organization responsible for this document says that of course, the government has taken very hard measures of restraint, the results of which will be better assessed within a couple of years. Besides, this is what the report says on page 30-as a matter of fact, it is the quotation the members of the opposition brought up on several occasions, but

without mentioning where it came from-and I quote:
-further fiscal and monetary restraint could conceivably result simply in higher rates of unemployment and economic slack with no more than marginal effects on current rates of increase in prices and costs.
That is merely an assumption, but when one is about to drown, one grabs the first branch available. Doing nothing does not help. Further on, we can read, and I quote:
Moreover, tight restraint in Canada this year is likely to have its main impact on the economy next year.
We shall see next year. When I hear members of the opposition criticize everything, I think we simply must do something. They are asking the government to engage in expenditures and investments that would reach several billion dollars but they have no practical answer to suggest.
The Creditiste member, at least, suggest a solution in which they believe since they have been upholding it for years, in the face of those who term it illusive.
I give them credit for that: they at least have a solution to suggest while most other members of the opposition are content with fighting against the government without proposing concrete solutions.
We are not playing at demagoguery, even though it would be easy to do so when there is unrest throughout the world and even in Canada. It is easy to play the demagogue, to set those who are the least informed in public affairs against the government, by claiming that the government in power it to blame for the unrest in the nation, as it has been done in other countries, without however solving any problem.
I heard the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) say: If things keep up this way, we will have a $12 billion budget this year. So what? The federal government gave more than ever to the provinces this year; the population has increased, as well as the needs and the cost of the social services. Had the government not imposed an austerity program, what would then be the situation! The government is blamed for being strict in its management of public funds and at the same time, it is blamed for curtailing expenses. Such is the logic of the members of the opposition. For instance, the government is taken to task for its failure to maintain certain positions which are not essential and, finally, for cutting down the number of some others.
December 11, 1969

[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is even blamed for having some thirty assistants at his disposal. But with his assistants, he works indeed. He has done more in one year than the opposition during all the time it was in office. It is constructive work and not necessarily party-oriented.
The hon. member for Edmonton West said that the public debt was increasing at an alarming rate. Federal and provincial governments, municipalities and school boards receive 45 cents out of every taxpayer dollar. He did not say however how much money found its way back into the taxpayers' pocket under the form of hospital insurance scheme, unemployment insurance benefits, old age pensions, pensions for disabled people, family allowances, and so on, and also under the form of assistance to universities and for the construction of hospitals and schools. You get nothing for nothing. In my opinion, the opposition could not make any miracle. If it wanted to meet the needs of the whole Canadian population, it would have to find the money where it is. Since it is not economical to manufacture synthetic gold, one must get it where it is.
I agree with some opposition members who feel that we should find ways to lighten the buren of the less fortunate taxpayers and to improve the lot of the unemployed. The members opposite will at least recognize that something new has been done: the designated areas have been delineated in a much more logical way than before. The granting of additional subsidies of more than $300 million has been approved to help the areas most affected by unemployment.
In my view, this measure is much more serious and its purpose is to eliminate poverty. It is much more efficient than the dreams and the lucubrations of certain quacks who pretend to solve everything here by condemning the government and laying at its door all the ills of mankind.
The situation is a difficult one, indeed. This government had the courage to enforce hard measures just before the elections and the Canadian people understood, as shown by the number of government members who were elected. We will complete the task. In spite of the lamentations of the Opposition members we will not stop until we have brought some stability to our economy, which will be achieved within a year, if I go by the quotation I read earlier.
Income Tax Act
I wish to ask the Opposition members to forget for a moment that we are poli.icians and that we may have different opinions on election matters. Let us remember, however, some fundamentals. We are first of all heads of families, responsible Canadians who want this country to survive, in the best way possible, even if, like individuals, it sometimes knows economic or other crises. When the economic climate is not the most favourable, it is not the right moment to say, as to a patient on the eve of an operation: I have seen many who have died of this. That would be encouraging! On the contrary, we must work hand in hand and tell the patient to cheer him up: Take courage and follow the doctor's advice even if it hurts. You will make it. This is what the people must be told, instead of being served a lot of baloney. They must be told to make sacrifices, because they have to in the circumstances.
We are going through a crisis, but we are weathering it better than any other country in the world. We are about to solve our economic problems. And we shall settle them before any other country in the world. All Canadians of good faith will agree on that. We shall discuss details when the crisis is over.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us is called:
"an act to amend an act to amend the Income Tax Act."
Although the scope of the amendment is quite broad, it can be summed up quite briefly, and I quote:
The purpose of this bill is to extend for one year the temporary surtaxes imposed in 1968 under Part IA of the Income Tax Act.
The surtax on an individual is 3%-
The surtax on a corporation is 3% of its tax computed under section 39 or 69 of the Income Tax Act.
Mr. Speaker, this act was adopted initially in 1968, and if my memory does not fail me, this bill was the occasion of the government's defeat by a vote taken here in the House, while we had agreed to support the government if the famous 5 per cent tax, in the form proposed, was not brought again before the House.
Now, after the distinct promises of the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and the Minister of National Revenue, the notorious bill levying an additional tax of 5 per cent was not introduced. However, immediately after the election, the government proposed a temporary surtax of 3

December 11, 1S69
Income Tax Act
per cent. We fought it then, and we will continue to fight any tax increases.
We, of the Ralliement creditiste, are accused of always talking about money, and of always repeating the same thing. But if we consider the contents of Bill C-139, we can say the same of the government, because this bill is the exact replica of a bill introduced last year and the preceding year.
We are asked to approve the extension of the temporary surtax of 3 per cent for one more year.
Mr. Speaker, at a time when prices are going up, when the government itself complains about inflation, it offers as a solution something which amounts to a reduction in purchasing power. How can we restore the economic balance and ensure markets for Canadian products while taking away from Canadians part of their purchasing power and at the same time telling them that it is indeed to fight inflation?
A moment ago I heard the member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) say: I was against the temporary surtax when I was sitting as an independent, but I changed my mind because I consider that the 3 per cent surtax is a good thing. And to prove that it is a good thing, he added that he was elected with a majority of 2,000 as an independent, whereas he had a majority of 7,000 as a Liberal.
At this stage, I would like-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Trois-Rivieres rises on a question of privilege.

My hon. friend generally is very clever and sharp of hearing, but I must point out to him that I have never said that the 3 per cent tax was a boon. I said rather that it was a necessary evil. There is a slight difference.

A necessary evil is a boon, whether we like it or not.
If the member for Trois-Rivieres enjoyed a majority of 7,000 votes at the last election, it is not due to the 3 per cent temporary surtax and probably not to the Liberal party's platform either.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Although I do not endorse the political ideas of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres

(Mr. Mongrain), I admit that his personality probably helped him getting elected in his area and not the popularity of the 3 per cent surtax. I challenge him to convince his constituents that such a surtax is a necessary evil.
The workers at the Trois-Rivieres plants in the hon. member's constituency are certainly opposed to this 3 per cent surtax and he knows that they need their whole income, that they already have too little. At the very moment when the hon. member is stating that this surtax is a necessary evil, his own constituents have to borrow from finance companies, to pledge their future wages in order to buy goods that were produced last year or will be produced this year.
And after having mortgaged their salaries for the next three or five years, these same workers look at the shelves of all the stores in Trois-Rivieres and find that they are filled more than ever before, even more than before they borrowed money from finance companies.
Is it a necessary evil or a solution to inflation to compel people to pay 15 or 18 p. 100 interest on loans from finance companies? And the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres will contend that the government is stabilizing the Canadian economy?
The government is stealing from the Canadian people. That is what it is doing.
Mr. Speaker, will the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) permit me a very short question?
Certainly, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Trois-Rivieres wishes to ask a question.
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to ask the hon. member for Temiscamingue if in his business a finance company does not finance the cars he sells.

Of course, but that is not my fault but rather the fault of people like the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, if we are compelled to impose taxes and to demand high interests to our clients, because we have to live in this system.
Personally, I am not out of this system, I am inside it. But, at least, I have the courage and the spirit to want to get out of it, while the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres wants to
December 11, 1969

maintain the people in this damnable stagnation that now prevails in Canada. That is the difference between the two of us.
Mr. Speaker, I did not introduce this system, and neither do I tolerate nor promote it. But the member for Trois-Rivieres is among those who are responsible for the present system and I want the constituents of his riding to know it once for all.
Mention was made earlier of the report of the Economic Council of Canada which said that it might be necessary to consider seriously the Canadian monetary question. It is no longer possible to govern under the present financial system.
I just read yesterday in a Montreal newspaper that all the municipalities of the city of Montreal show at present a deficit of $6,225,000. The municipalities have to pay or to contribute, to the debt service only, 60 per cent of the municipal budget.
And we would consider as adequate a system which obliges us to levy 3 per cent surtax-which is called "a necessary evil" in order again to drain the taxpayers of their income and the Canadian consumers of their purchasing power.
We are told: Let us try it for one year and we shall see what happens. What were the results of this tax approved by parliament last year? Inflation is worse today than it was a year ago. Restrictions were imposed on municipalities, school boards and provinces.
A federal-provincial conference on the constitutionality and distribution of the tax base in Canada has just ended.
They quarrelled about taxation rights. One by one, the provinces told the federal government: We have had enough of Canada's taxation power. The federal government answered: We need it, we shall levy taxes and then we shall distribute this money to the people.
Mr. Speaker, that has always been done in Canada, there has been taxation but when the time came to distribute the money to the people, the failure was complete on all fronts, even if it is said today that, in consequence, we have social security. I could speak all night on the subject of social security and on the way it is administered in Quebec and in other Canadian provinces. Mothers are compelled to humiliate themselves in government offices, to make known their poverty, in a country where there is an abundance of resources of all kinds. For this, they are given the measly sum of $105, $110 or $125 per
Income Tax Act
month to support their spouse and five, six or seven children.
If that is economic stability, if that is the just society, I wonder where we are heading with the solutions now proposed by the government.
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres has nevertheless been honest enough to say that the Ralliement creditiste proposes a solution to that problem. What are we suggesting? We suggest the opposite of what the government proposes by pretending to spend according to the taxes collected. The limit of expenses should be in accordance with the taxation system. If we tax for $10 billion, let us limit our expenses to $10 billion. And meanwhile production surpluses are piling up in factories, in shops, at the wholesalers, in warehouses, everywhere in Canada.
Recently I had the opportunity to visit Western Canada. There is too much wheat in Western Canada and too much wood in British Columbia. In Ontario there is too much corn in the Toronto area and too much wood in Northern Ontario. In Quebec there is too much milk and too many other products. In fact the farmers were here only two days ago to acquaint us of their problems concerning milk surpluses. If we go to the Maritimes, we find there is an overproduction of fish, pulp, and potatoes in New Brunswick, as well as in Prince Edward Island. In this situation, the government says: our spending power lies in taxation. And what do we reply? We say that a responsible government should recognize that its spending power lies in the country's production potential, that our expenditures should be based on our production.
If we produce goods worth $72 billion, we should issue enough credit to let our production reach the Canadian consumers. Then poverty would be efficiently done away with.
But Creditiste proposals are rather laughed at when they simply call on the governments to do in peacetime what they did so well in wartime. When we entered the war in 1939, under a liberal government, it was then said: Let us make financially possible what is physically workable. The first thing the Mackenzie King government did was to create, through the hon. J. L. Ilsley, Minister of Finance, to have the Bank of Canada issue 200 million dollars' worth of new, interest-free credits, to be used to start manufacturing guns, shells, destructive weapons and to "clothe" our young men who had gone naked for ten years, feed and house them, and pay

December 11, 1969
Income Tax Act
them besides to go forth and defend Christendom and civilization.
At that time, the services of the Bank of Canada were called upon, but when it comes to keeping our population alive, of allowing our young students to integrate into our present Canadian civilization, the government is powerless. Then we are told that we must accept what has become a necessary evil, last year a 3 per cent tax which was to be temporary, but which is still temporary this year and will be temporary next year again, and no doubt plus an increase, and all this in order to fight inflation.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, that is what we are so dead against, we, of the Ralliement creditiste. By the way, if the government can find millions to destroy, he should find some to allow the people to live.
The spending power of a responsible government and a sovereign government that wishes to discharge its responsibilities is its production power. To the extent that we can produce, let us organize a financial system able to allow the production to reach the consumer. How can we reach that goal? Simply by imposing a 3 per cent tax? Indeed not, but rather by distributing a national dividend to each and every Canadian citizen. This dividend has been laughed at, and it can still be laughed at, but there is only one way to find markets for the stockpile of products now existing in Canada: increase the purchasing power of Canadian consumers. And when we can do this without boosting taxes, we shall have found a solution. Of course, if we increase taxes or adopt the government's method which consists in taking from those who have and give to those who do not, the over-all purchasing power of the population will not be increased.
If a Canadian earns $8,000 a year and I take $1,500 or $2,000 from him and give it to someone else, the purchasing power is the same, that is $8,000 for two instead of only one. In the circumstances, we know very well that the one who earns $8,000 a year cannot afford to hide some of it under his mattress because he needs it all to support his family and buy a house which he cannot even afford to pay cash, and that in turn forces him to contract a loan with a finance company for the next 25, 30 or 40 years.
So, those who have a little more are deprived of their purchasing power in favour of those who have less; that is what is called State socialism or, better still, rank commu-IMr. Caouette.l
nism. This is what they are forcing us to put up with. Mr. Speaker, such solutions we can do without.
If we deprive someone of his assets to help a have-not, we will weaken the individual incentive which a government such as ours should encourage in its own interest. The measures proposed by this government surely do not encourage individual effort, any more than they encourage private or free entreprise.
Let us come back to our solution. Instead of allowing the levy of a temporary tax of 3 per cent, we will oppose it with our utmost energy as we will support the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), which proposes to postpone for six months the passage of this bill. We feel that the government should find sources of revenue elsewhere than in the purse of the modest taxpayer or the Canadian consumer.
We have in Canada a most excellent institution. People may laugh, but the Bank of Canada can be used to such ends as it was used for military purposes in 1939. If the Bank of Canada must reflect the economic growth of Canada, it is up to the government to have the Bank realize financially what is physically possible.
Canadians in the Trois-Rivieres riding, as well as miners in Rouyn-Noranda, and workers and farmers in the St-Maurice region are ready to roll up their sleeves and to produce more.
Increasing production in Canada is not a problem. All our producers, all our manufacturers are prepared to increase their production, but the fact is that the government, with outdated measures, with measures that make no sense, bring them to a standstill by saying: listen, you have too much wheat, too much lumber, too much milk, too much of this and that. On the other hand, he tells them: we can improve the standard of living of the Canadian people inasmuch as we increase productivity. One day, production must be increased, and the next day production is too high, and since there is overproduction the government will have to tax more under the pretence of fighting inflation which, in my opinion, is due to the fact that the buying power exceeds the quality of products available, which causes a shortage.
If the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres takes his Larousse dictionary, and he used to be a teacher, he will see that inflation is to have worthless money when a shortage of products prevails.
December 11, 1969

What is the situation today? Is it that the 180,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec have too much money in their pockets, Mr. Speaker? Is it that the families living from social welfare have too much money? Is it that the poor people in Canada have too much money in their pockets? No, they have too little. Would a single hon. member say that he has too much money? No, but at least he has a little. It is a little too much to try to convince the poor that he has too much money.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployed in Canada, the hopelessly destitute need some purchasing power to get the necessary goods. The problem today is not excess money, but scarce money, considering the huge production in all fields and sectors of the economic activity in Canada.
The members of the Ralliement creditiste have been making suggestions for a long time. People refuse to listen to them in their own interests. In the lobbies, some liberal or progressive conservative members sometimes tell us: Boys, you are right, but we can do nothing. We are committed.
We, of the Ralliement creditiste, are not committed to anything. We are free to say what we please. It is our right. We are at liberty to say what we think, point out authentic facts to members of parliament, and nobody can deny us that right, not even the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, and that, even if he tells us that we live in a fool's paradise and dream in colour.
At least, we dream of something, while the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres does not even seem able to dream.
This being said, I suggest that the solution to the current problem is not to increase taxes, but to reduce them, in order to give the consumers greater purchasing power, which will enable them to get the goods and services offered them.
Nowadays, builders, manufacturers and producers are penalized and they are told: Restraints on credit prevent us to undertake such project or to take action in such a field. Why should we go and get credit in the U.S.A. instead of creating it at home out of nothing? This credit would be guaranteed by the goods we can produce and the natural resources we can develop in Canada.
Recently, the N.D.P. government of Manitoba boasted that it had borrowed $15 million in the United States at 8.89 per cent. These $15 million did not exist in Canada before the
Income Tax Act
Minister of Finance of Manitoba borrowed them. Had the Bank of Canada created that money, would that have been more inflationary?
No, because the Manitoba government would have obtained the same amount but interest free. It would have been also used to build an hydro-electric complex in that province. It seems to me that this would have been more logical than to kneel submissively to American capitalists who, themselves, have created the necessary credit to get rich with the help of Canadian manpower and brain power.
Besides, as the Economic Council of Canada stated, as long as the monetary system is not changed, we will barely manage to live in a state of stagnation. We are ready to reform the institutions and to ask the citizens to reform. In fact, we ask the Canadian people to tighten their belt by requiring the payment of a 3 per cent temporary surtax for a year. At the same time, we say to financiers and others: Lend money at a higher interest rate. This is the government solution.
As was mentioned recently by a senator, the rich get richer in smaller number and the poor get poorer in greater number.
When the people become tired of that system and really understand the part played by finance, those who do not serve the people will be kicked out of the House of Commons and of the legislatures.
The solution that we propose is in no way miraculous. Credit is created by men like all of us, like the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres or like any other member. Those are men who draw up the financial and monetary policy of Canada, and when they will have realized the necessity of an adequate monetary system, geared to the needs of our population, according to the goods produced by it, then bills like Bill C-139 will no longer be introduced in this House.

I say it again the Creditistes will not perform miracles. But I must say the present government does not perform many either. They refuse to do anything.
When the Prime Minister of a sovereign state says that he does not have the means to solve problems, except through taxation, I say that government shirks its obligations. It is time for a government, supported by a Parliament made up of reasonable men, to

I heard a while ago a conservative member blaming the Liberals. The Progressive Conservatives governed this country from 1957 to 1962. Did they do any better? In 1960-61, there were a million unemployed in Canada. What did the Progressive Conservatives do to cope with unemployment then? They say there is unemployment, there is abundance and there is poverty. There is a severe housing crisis, a lack of this and that. Maybe the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) can still remember, but as for the others, I doubt it.
As for us, we do have a solution and we will keep on proposing it until it is applied. We should certainly give it a try. And if it does not prove to be good, let us put it aside.
As the present Postmaster General and Minister of Communications said, people voted for Social Credit because they were told all about the lack of money. The minister explained it all in 1964 to the students of McGill University in Montreal while telling them about the Creditiste phenomenon, the Caouette phenomenon in Quebec.
He said: While we refrained from talking about money, Caouette spoke of the lack of money. That caught on in the Dorchester and Trois-Rivieres areas. That was to be known as the Creditiste phenomenon. The hon. minister said: "Scarce money or tight money is a bad thing."
That is exactly where we stand today and the Creditistes are not to blame for a situation that has brought about interest rates as high as 10 and 12 per cent. It is the government that should get the blame.
Today, the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications, an economist to boot, and former president of the Montreal Exchange, not only does not rise to fight Bill C-139 but he will vote for it tomorrow or the day after, while in 1964 he condemned the same method. Therefore, he has the same

attitude as the member for Trois-Rivieres. In 1964, both were against. Today, they have changed their minds, but not for partisan reasons they say. I do not know for whom the 3 per cent surtax has become a necessary evil. Certainly not for workers, farmers, white-collar or blue-collar workers. It can only serve the ends of a barbarian financial system that fleeces the entire Canadian population.
Mr. Speaker, we will continue to demand security with personal freedom through the establishment of a system promoting personal effort instead of discouraging it and protecting free enterprise instead of stifling and crushing it. We might have to wait 10, 15 or 20 years to make this clear to the people. We will take the time we need, but Canada will eventually have a Creditiste government making money available to the individual, which is the object of Bill C-139 now under consideration.

Mr. Speaker, it seems fitting that the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) and I should carry on in the pre-midnight hours in this pre-Christmas season with a discussion on Christmas mail. I wish to recall that some time ago I asked about the announcement he made outside the House that there would be three Saturday deliveries preceding Christmas. While at first blush the minister may look like a latter day Kris Kringle, I think in fact this is an indication that the non-movement on Saturday has been a great contributor to the deterioration of the mail service.
Hear, hear.

In other words, it was palpably necessary to reinstitute the Saturday movement of mail in order to move the heavy volume of mail in the Christmas season. It follows I am sure-and I have information which leads me to believe it is true-that were it not for the blocking-out of the Saturday morning delivery, the other movements would have been more satisfactory since the minister adopted this ill-advised and ill-considered move. I note, too, the generosity with which he referred to the cost of $350,000. There have been discussions later than that date about the payments made for overtime work.
I am convinced that the five-day delivery has been a major contributor, if not the major contributor, to the unhappy state of the Post Office. So often mail which is found in the Post Office on Monday cannot be processed in time for Monday's delivery, and it is quite possible that many many articles of mail are in fact not moved from Friday to Tuesday. Therefore, I do not think it is surprising that people still complain in increasing volume about the slowness of the mail delivery.
I think all members of this House receive a consistent and indeed increasing flow of mail complaining about the mail service. One has only to look at the editorials, and letters to the editor in the newspapers to get an indication of just what is going on. I only wish we had some system of slides, dials or something whereby we could register in this chamber

It may be the age of expedition but it is certainly not the age of transmission of mail. This whole business of Saturday mail delivery has been a preposterous fiasco from the beginning.
If you live in rural Canada you get mail six days a week; if you live in urban Canada you get it five days a week. But try getting a stamp a little cheaper if you happen to live in rural Canada. The charge is the same, but the service is different. This is one of the great contributions to the unhappy situation which prevails in the Post Office, and I am being as charitable as I can in view of the approaching yuletide. This distortion,, this ridiculous discrimination between rural and urban people, and the foolish notion that you can move more mail in five days than you can in six, is preposterous. I say to the minister that one of the legacies which he will leave to the Crown corporation, if and when it is put into being to clean up the mess in which the Post Office is now, will result from this five day delivery.
I say to him that had he recognized long before Christmas that the system was not working, things would be much better now. There would be far fewer users of the mail writing to their members complaining about the mail, and there might be suggestions

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, your consistent suggestions that the questions of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) could be more appropriately dealt with at the time of adjournment reflect not only your desire to avoid wasting the time of this House but also your impatience with the repetitious nature of his questions.

Saturday delivery during the Christmas season costs the people of Canada approximately $350,000 per day. The hon. member suggests that this be repeated 52 times a year. Today's task force report on the future of the Canada Post Office points out the impact of rising costs on the price of mailing first-class letters-26 cents per letter in less than a generation. That is what we in the Post Office want to avoid, by trying to equalize the amount of services rendered with their cost.
The hon. member has referred to me as a constitutional diplomat, Kris Kringle, and so on. Watching and listening to his performance this evening I thought of the character in that wonderful Shakespearean play "A Midsummer-Night's Dream", of which his former leader is so fond. The hon. member for Hillsborough would be very ably cast as "Bottom," but a blushing Bottom in this instance; for he is blushing as one who knows he lacks conviction in his cause and knows clearly he is saying nothing that he has not said many times before.
There is no Saturday urban delivery and will not be, except for Christmas, until the Canadian taxpayer says he is willing to subsidize Canadian business for 80 per cent of the cost of such a service. There will not be this service until the Canadian taxpayer says that there are not better ways of spending 52 times $350,000 a year, for example, on such things as housing, welfare, health, regional development, or any of the very many other needs that the Canadian people have. I plead with the hon. member to not only avoid the Christmas blush of always being late but also the Conservative blush, the blush of living in a day that is long past.

Mr. Speaker, after that very fine display of oratory from both sides of the House I am afraid I must come down to some very simple probing which has to do with Christmas toys. It is now three weeks since Dr. Morton Shulman, former Toronto coroner and now a member of the Ontario legislature, raised the matter of the potential killer toy, the Poweride Car, which could have caused serious injury or death to a Montreal child when the sulphuric acid in its battery leaked out. It is two weeks since I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) about the matter in this House. I drew to his attention the fact that an official of his department accompanied a member of the Canadian Toy Testing Council and that they saw no hazard in this toy car.
My interest stems from the fact that a lot of parents around the country are living in a fool's paradise. They believe themselves to be properly protected against buying dangerous toys. Actually, they have no such protection at all. So far as I can learn the only testing now carried out is done through the Canadian Toy Testing Council. I want to point out several things about that council. First of all, it is a purely voluntary body, composed of 17 people, mostly women who have a great many other responsibilities, and they do the testing. In the second place, the council can test only a very limited number of toys each year. They are up against all the resources of a multi-million dollar industry.
A third point which has not yet been raised is that they receive a grant of $500 a year from the Canadian Toy Manufacturers' Association, and one could hardly call that a disinterested grant. It is probably hush money, but it did not hush-up the sulphuric acid when it leaked out of the battery of that toy car in Montreal. In the fourth place, the council receives no assistance whatsoever from the department. Maybe it gets moral backing, but moral backing is not worth much when they do not have the financial backing necessary to test toys.
I want to show the result of the council not having had backing from the department. On November 25 a member of the Toy Testing Council, Mrs. P. J. Pocock, made a statement which, curiously enough, was released by Eldon Industries of Canada, Ltd., the Canadian subsidiary of the U.S. based manufacturer

who produced the Eldon Poweride Car that nearly killed the Montreal child. I quote part of Mrs. Pocock's statement as follows:
"I examined the car in the company of an official of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and could see no hazard to a child under normal use. The same conclusion was reached by the officer of Consumer Affairs," Mrs. Pocock is quoted as having declared.

Eldon Industries of Canada president and general manager Dennis E. Tiberis insists that 'we are certain it is perfectly safe for children to use.
'Almost 200,000 of these cars have already been sold in the United States and have been in use for several months, and we know of no instances of children being harmed in any way,' he said.
The matter was raised in the Ontario legislature. It was also raised in this House, and around the beginning of this month the T. Eaton Company Limited took the car off the market, having become convinced that it was not a safe car for small children. On December 5 another statement was made by Mrs. A. B. R. Mr. Speaker, on December 8 I asked the Minister of Na.ional Defence (Mr. Cadieux) a question which was prompted by a statement which appeared in the St. John's newspaper on December 4 to the effect the Canadian Armed Forces are very much interested in taking over the Argeniia naval base if and when the Un.ted Slates decides to withdraw from that base.
We are all aware that some time ago a statement was made by the government of the Uni.ed States to the effect that some 300 U.S. bases were being phased out around the world. Shortly after that statement was released, over 200 people-260,1 believe-who were working on the Argentia naval base were paid off, which led people to believe that Argentia would be one of the bases that would be phased out amongst the 309 announced by the United States Secretary of Defence.
This is a very serious situation, Mr. Speaker. At the present time there are over 800 people working on that base. The economy of the entire area of Placentia Bay is fairly well dependent on the base. There is not a family in that whole area that does not in some way or ano.her derive a living from this United States base. For that reason I was delighted to read in the newspaper that according to ViceAdmiral O'Brien, Commanding Officer of the Canadian Forces Base at Halifax, the Canadian Forces may be interested in taking over Argentia if and when the United States decides to phase it out.
I have directed a number of questions in this House to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) asking what information he had received from his counterpart in the United S ates government with respect to the future of this and other bases in Canada. The answer has always been the same, that he has not received any indication from the United States authorities that Argentia will be phased out. I say to the minister and this House that there are very strong indications that the base will be phased out on June 30, 1970. It is about time the Minister of National Defence or his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, put the question to their counterparts in the Uni ed States government and found out once and for all where we stand with regard to United States bases in Newfoundland.

As I mentioned earlier, if and when these bases are phased out the social and economic consequences could be very tragic so far as the people in that area are concerned. I do not ihink it is enough for this government and the ministers involved to adopt the old ostrich psychology of sticking their heads in the sand and hoping nothing will happen. I think it is obvious to all of us, par icularly the people in my riding, that the Argentia naval base is going to be phased out. I thunk the time has come for us to find out what is going to happen. The federal government, and other levels of government should start making plans to provide o.her employment if and when this base is phased out.
We have had two very tragic events in Newfoundland in the last ten years. The closing of Pepperrell Air Force base left a large number of people unemployed. The la er closing of Ernest Harmon Air Force base had very tragic effects on the area in and around Harmon Field and indeed all over Newfoundland. As the member for St. John's West, in whose riding the Argentia naval base is situated, I am not prepared to stand by and see the same thing happen. I do not ihink the people of the area deserve that treatment. I call upon the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to put ihe question directly to the United States authorities.
